name: William Simon

summary.text: William E. Simon, a former Salomon Brothers bond trader, was U.S. Treasury Secretary from 1974 to 1977. According to Bloomberg's 2016 account based on documents released under the Freedom of Information Act, Simon travelled to Jeddah in July 1974 on a mission to persuade Saudi Arabia to finance U.S. deficits with its petrodollar revenues in exchange for preferential access to Treasury securities, an arrangement the Saudis insisted be kept secret; Treasury disclosed Saudi holdings, then about $117 billion, for the first time in 2016.

facts.claim: In July 1974 Treasury Secretary Simon travelled to Saudi Arabia on what was officially a diplomacy tour, with the goal of neutralising crude oil as an economic weapon and persuading the kingdom to finance America's widening deficit with its petrodollar wealth.
facts.quote: neutralize crude oil as an economic weapon and find a way to persuade a hostile kingdom to finance America's widening deficit with its newfound petrodollar wealth

sources.title: The untold story behind Saudi Arabia's 41-year US debt secret

facts.claim: Under the arrangement Bloomberg described, Saudi Arabia would invest oil revenue in U.S. debt in exchange for preferential access to Treasury securities, and insisted the arrangement be kept secret for fear of being seen as supporting U.S. aid to Israel.
facts.quote: insisted it be kept secret due to fears that it would be perceived to being "directly or indirectly" supporting US financial aid to Israel

connections.claim: Simon negotiated with Saudi Arabia in 1974 an arrangement under which the kingdom would buy U.S. Treasury securities with oil revenue, according to Bloomberg's account of FOIA-released documents.

openQuestions: The site says Saudi Arabia was offered 'a confidential way to buy Treasuries outside the auctions' (add-on purchases). The sources found describe 'preferential access' without specifying the add-on mechanism; that detail is in Bloomberg's original article (bloomberg.com, May 30, 2016), which was unreachable.
Sources used are syndications of the Bloomberg article; the original should be cited.
